ABSTRACT
Background: Antibodies against glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD-abs) at high serum levels are associated with
diverse autoimmune neurological syndromes (AINS), including cerebellar ataxia, epilepsy, limbic encephalitis
and stiff-person syndrome. The impact of low serum GAD-ab levels in patients with suspected AINS remains
controversial. Specific intrathecal GAD-ab synthesis may serve as a marker for GAD-ab-associated nervous system
autoimmunity. We present characteristics of a multicentric patient cohort with suspected AINS associated with
GAD antibodies (SAINS-GAD + ) and explore the relevance of serum GAD-ab levels and intrathecal GAD-ab
synthesis.
Methods: All patients with SAINS-GAD + included in the registry of the German Network for Research on
Autoimmune Encephalitis (GENERATE) from 2011 to 2019 were analyzed. High serum GAD-ab levels were
defined as RIA > 2000 U/mL, ELISA > 1000 U/mL, or as a positive staining pattern on cell-based assays.
Results: One-hundred-one patients were analyzed. In descending order they presented with epilepsy/limbic en -
cephalitis (39%), cerebellar ataxia (28%), stiff person syndrome (22%), and overlap syndrome (12%). Immu -
notherapy was administered in 89% of cases with improvements in 46%. 35% of SAINS-GAD + patients had low
GAD-ab serum levels. Notably, unmatched oligoclonal bands in CSF but not in serum were more frequent in
patients with low GAD-ab serum levels. GAD-ab-levels (high/low) and intrathecal GAD-ab synthesis (present or
not) did not impact clinical characteristics and outcome.
Conclusions: Overall, immunotherapy in SAINS-GAD + was moderately effective. Serum GAD-ab levels and the
absence or presence of intrathecal GAD-ab synthesis did not predict clinical characteristics or outcomes in SAINS-
GAD + . The detection of unmatched oligoclonal bands might outweigh low GAD-ab serum levels.
1. Introduction
Antibodies (abs) against the enzyme glutamic acid decarboxylase 65
(GAD-abs) are established markers of insulin-dependent diabetes mel -
litus [ 1 ] and are also associated with diverse autoimmune neurological
syndromes (AINS), typically presenting with (i) cerebellar ataxia (CAT)
[ 2 ] (ii) epilepsy (E), mainly of temporal lobe origin [ 3 ] and limbic en -
cephalitis (LE) [ 4 , 5 ] as well as (iii) stiff-person syndrome (SPS) [ 6 ]
including progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus
(PERM) [ 7 ] and (iv) overlap of these syndromes [ 8 ]. In contrast to the
experience in AINS associated with abs against surface antigens [ 9 ], the
effectiveness of immunotherapy in GAD-abs associated AINS appears
poor and a chronic course is often observed [ 8 , 10 , 11 ].
Although GAD-abs were first described 30 years ago, their patho -
genic and diagnostic relevance in AINS is still a matter of debate [ 1 , 12 ].
Since GAD-ab levels in AINS were reported to be 10-100fold higher than
in patients with diabetes mellitus [ 1 ], it was hypothesized that GAD-ab
levels correlate with the likelihood of a GAD-abs associated AINS. Of
note, the distinction of high vs. low GAD-ab serum levels was not based
on pathophysiological evidence [ 1 , 2 , 12 ], such that the relevance of
these levels in AINS are still matter of debate [ 13 ]. Furthermore, clear-
cut threshold values to discriminate between high-level and low-level
GAD-ab values have not been defined. Another relevant problem in
evaluating ab test results in general and for GAD-abs in particular is the
growing diversity of laboratory test methods. The increasing knowledge
about ab-associated AINS led to an enormous expansion of ab tests in
suspected patients in the last decade. While at the beginning ab tests
were performed in large international reference laboratories only, tests
in Germany are increasingly carried out decentrally in local laboratories
using commercially available test kits or in-house procedures. This
further complicates assessment of the relevance of positive ab findings
for the treating physicians. Methods for GAD-ab determination in clin -
ical routine are highly heterogeneous. Radio-immuno-assay (RIA),
enzyme-linked-immunosorbent assay (ELISA), and GAD-specific cell-
based-assays are used [ 13 – 15 ]. Tissue-based assays using immunohis -
tochemistry to detect typical staining patterns on rodent or non-human
primate brain tissue (and pancreas) supplement the specific test mo -
dalities. While results differ between laboratories within tests, com -
parison between different methods is even more problematic. Besides
GAD-ab levels, another promising marker for GAD-ab involvement in
AINS might be the intrathecal synthesis of GAD-abs [ 16 ].
In this study, we aimed to describe all patients with suspected AINS
associated with GAD antibodies (SAINS-GAD + ) included in the German
Network for Research on Autoimmune Encephalitis (GENERATE) to
reveal typical features of the individual syndromes involved and to
provide insights into current management. Further, we assessed the
relevance of GAD-ab levels and intrathecal GAD-ab synthesis from
routine diagnostics for the clinical management in a sizeable multi -
centric patient cohort of SAINS-GAD + .

2. Methods and materials
2.1. Study population and inclusion criteria
We reviewed all patients with SAINS-GAD + included in GENERATE,
a nationwide multicentric prospective non-interventional registry for
people with AINS in Germany ( https://generate-net.de ). The network
represents a free alliance of hospitals at different levels of care and is
thus suitable to reflect “ real world ” conditions for the management of
patients with AINS. The inclusion period ranged from 03/2011 to 04/
2019.
SAINS-GAD + encompassed the following neurological syndromes
previously associated with GAD-abs: E/LE, CAT, SPS/PERM and an
overlap of these syndromes. Since LE and temporal lobe epilepsy, as well
as SPS and PERM, were suspected to be variants of one syndrome each
[ 11 ], we merged them categorically in order to obtain sufficiently large
comparison subgroups.
Data documented at first presentation were: syndrome, age at onset,
disease duration, gender, autoimmune comorbidities, tumor identifica -
tion, routine cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) data (CSF pleocytosis ≥ 5 / μ l,
unmatched oligoclonal bands in CSF and the use of immunotherapy).
According to previous recommendations for the treatment of ab-
associated AINS [ 9 , 17 ], immunotherapy comprised as first-line regi -
mens intravenous high-dose methylprednisolone pulses, intravenous
immunoglobulins (IVIG), apheresis techniques including plasmaphe -
resis and immunoadsorption, and as second-line regimens cyclophos -
phamide and rituximab. Further, ongoing immunosuppression, in
addition to the immunotherapy mentioned above, was noted.
The outcome was evaluated in all patients with available follow-up
of at least three months following the first presentation. As outcome
parameters, we evaluated functional impairment using the modified
Rankin Scale (mRS): values from 0 to 1 were assigned as favorable, 2 – 3
as moderate, 4 – 5 as unfavorable, and 6 as fatal, i.e., dead. Further, mRS
improvement at the last follow-up compared to the maximum mRS level
at timepoint of diagnosis, and the proportion of patients free of any
symptom were assessed.
Of note, for patient enrollment in GENERATE, no cut-off values for
GAD-ab levels are defined. According to the GENERATE registry ’ s
multicentric non-interventional design, several established clinical lab -
oratory test procedures were employed for GAD-ab detection: RIA,
ELISA and cell-based assays (Euroimmun, Luebeck, Germany). All lab -
oratory data were extracted from clinical routine test results, as this
corresponds to the clinical reality according to which people with
SAINS-GAD + are classified and treated currently in Germany.
According to previous reports [ 14 , 18 ] laboratory criteria for quali -
fying GAD-ab as high-level were at least one of the following in serum:
RIA > 2000 IU/mL, ELISA > 1000 IU/mL, or cell-based assay ≥ 1:10. If
one of these laboratory criteria was fulfilled at the first presentation,
patients were classified as “ high-level ” (high-GAD-ab). If results were
below these cut-off values, patients were classified as “ low-level ” (low-
GAD-ab). In case of incomplete data for this categorization, patients
were excluded from this part of the analysis.
Intrathecal GAD-ab synthesis was calculated as described previously
[ 16 ]. Parameters had to be tested at the same time. Values > 1 for were
rated as positive for intrathecal GAD-ab synthesis [ 19 ].
2.2. Ethics
All participants or their legal representatives gave written informed
consent. Initial institutional review board approval was granted by the
ethical advisory board of the University of Luebeck, Germany (reference
number: 13 – 162) and consecutively by all participating centers ’
regional ethical advisory boards.
2.3. Statistics
Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS for Windows (IBM,
Armonk, New York, USA). For comparisons of independent categorical
data, the chi-square test or Fisher ’ s exact test (if less than five items) were
performed for paired comparison and the Freeman-Halton-test for mul -
tiple comparisons. For independent metrical data, the Mann-Whitney- U
test was performed for paired comparisons and the Kruskal-Wallis-test for
multiple comparisons. To circumvent the problem of multiple compari -
sons, pairwise subgroup analyses were only performed if the overall effect
was significant with adjustment of p -values using the Bonferroni
correction. P -values < 0.05 were considered as statistically significant.
3. Results
3.1. Study population
We identified 101 patients with SAINS-GAD + from the database.
SAINS-GAD + patients presented most frequently with E/LE ( N = 39,
38.6%), followed by CAT ( N = 28, 27.7%), SPS/PERM ( N = 22, 21.8%),
and an overlap of these syndromes ( N = 12, 11.9%). GAD-ab positivity
in SAINS-GAD + patients was assessed by RIA in 30 cases (29.7%), by
ELISA in 33 cases (32.7%), and by cell-based assay in 38 cases (37.6%).
A concurrent autoimmune disease was present in 49 patients
(48.5%). Diabetes mellitus was found frequently (44.9%), but the most
commonly associated autoimmune disease was autoimmune thyroiditis
(53.1%). A malignancy was found in only 2/64 patients evaluated
(3.1%): uterine cancer (N = 1) and breast cancer (N = 1). In none of the
patients, further specific abs associated with AINS were found.
The majority of patients was treated with immunotherapy ( N = 90,
89.1%), regularly with multiple consecutive regimens ( N = 69, 76.7%).
Chronic immunosuppression was additionally given in 25/101 patients
(24.8%). In addition to first-line regimens, in 30 patients (30%) second-
line regimens were used, cyclophosphamide was only given adjunctive
to rituximab. Bortezomib and basiliximab were given as off-label uses in
one patient each, adjunctive to rituximab, because of severity of this
disease.
Follow-up was available in 79 patients (78.2%). The mRS at the last
follow-up compared to the acute stage had improved in 36/79 cases
(45.6%), however the outcome was moderate in most patients (57.0%),
and complete symptom remission was achieved rarely (5.1%).
Table 1 summarizes all characteristics of the study population.
3.2. Characteristics of SAINS-GAD + subgroups
E/LE comprised of 39 patients, the largest subgroup in SAINS-GAD + .
Seizures were present in 34 patients (87.2%) and the only symptom in 5
patients (12.8%). Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was abnormal in
23/37 patients (62.2%), including T2-hyperintensity, contrast
enhancement, swelling, or atrophy. In most cases solely temporal
structures were involved ( N = 20/23, 87.0%), combined temporal and
extratemporal pathology was present in 1/23 (4.3%), and extratemporal
pathology only in 2/23 patients (8.7%). Electroencephalography (EEG)
was found pathological in 28/37 cases (75.7%), with temporal abnor -
malities in 26/28 patients (92.9%) and with extratemporal pathology in
2/28 patients (7.1%).
CAT represented the second most frequent SAINS-GAD + in our
cohort ( N = 28). MRI displayed cerebellar atrophy in only 7/25 cases
(28.0%). In this subgroup, EEG was obtained infrequently (6/28, 21.4%)
and was normal in all patients.
SPS was diagnosed in 22 patients (21.8%). MRI was abnormal in 1/
14 patients (7.1%) with temporal pathology, EEG was normal in all
evaluated cases (0/2).

An overlap syndrome was present in 12 patients encompassing the
following combinations: E/LE-CAT in 6 (50.0%), SPS-CAT in 3 (25.0%),
E/LE-SPS in 2 patients (16.7%) and one patient had a triad of E/LE-CAT-
SPS (8.3%). MRI was pathological in 4/9 overlap patients (44.4%): three
with temporal and one with diffuse lesions. EEG was abnormal in 4/7
cases (57.1%), all with temporal localization.
3.3. Comparison of SAINS-GAD + subgroups
Median age at onset of patients with E/LE was lower than in patients
with CAT ( p ≤ 0.001). Median disease duration at first presentation was
longer for patients with SPS than for the E/LE and CAT subgroups (SPS
vs. E/LE, p = 0.007; vs. CAT p = 0.03). Maximum mRS at the timepoint
of diagnosis was higher in CAT and SPS than in E/LE ( p = 0.001, each).
Regarding outcome parameters, only mRS in SPS at follow-up was
higher than in E/LE ( p = 0.01). All other parameters did not differ when
syndromic subgroups were compared.
Table 2 displays the characteristics and comparisons of the syndro -
matic subgroups of SAINS-GAD + patients.
According to the presented clinical syndrome, the choice and extent
of immunotherapy regimens differed. Second-line regimens were more
often given in overlap than in the E/LE and SPS subgroups (vs. E/LE: p =
0.005; vs. SPS: p = 0.02). Methylprednisolone pulses were given pre -
dominantly in E/LE in 79.5% of cases (vs. CAT: 57.1%, p = 0.06; vs. SPS:
50.0%, p = 0.02; overlap: 41.7%, p = 0.03). Conversely, IVIG were
administered less frequently in E/LE (7.7%) than in the other syndromes
(vs. CAT: 50.0%, < 0.001; vs. SPS: 54.5%%, p < 0.001; vs. overlap:
41.7%; p = 0.01). Rituximab was predominantly used in overlap pa -
tients (66.7%; vs. E/LE: 20.5%, p = 0.005; vs. CAT: 35.7%, P = 0.09; vs.
SPS: 18.2%%, P = 0.008). Cyclophosphamide was applied more
frequently in CAT (14.3%) than in E/LE (0%, p = 0.03). Further details
are given in Supplemental Table 1.
3.4. Comparison of high- versus low-GAD-ab patients
In 97/101 (96.0%) patients serum GAD-ab levels could be catego -
rized, 63/97 patients (64.9%) fulfilled the criteria for high-GAD-ab,
whereas 34/97 patients (35.1%) were categorized as low-GAD-ab, for
details see Table 3 . Surprisingly, unmatched oligoclonal bands in CSF
occurred more frequently in low-GAD-ab ( N = 24/30, 80.0%) than in
high-GAD-ab ( N = 20/52, 38.5%; p < 0.001), but this remained without
differences in outcome. A favorable outcome was observed in 3/17
(18%) low-GAD patients with unmatched oligoclonal bands and in 3/5
(60%) low-GAD without unmatched oligoclonal bands ( p = 0.1). Intra -
thecal GAD-ab synthesis was more often seen in high-GAD-ab ( N = 23/
33, 69.7% vs. N = 1/19, 5.3%; p < 0.001). All other parameters did not
differ between the two subgroups.
3.5. Clinical correlation of intrathecal GAD-ab synthesis
The correlation of intrathecal GAD-ab synthesis to clinical syn -
dromes could be analyzed in 54/101 patients (53.5%), including 24
patients with intrathecal GAD-ab synthesis (44.4%). Intrathecal GAD-ab
synthesis differed according to SAINS-GAD + : the majority of E/LE pa -
tients were positive for intrathecal GAD-ab synthesis ( N = 16/22,
72.7%; p = 0.008) whereas most SPS patients were negative ( N = 9/10,
90.0%; p = 0.03). Patients without intrathecal GAD-ab synthesis showed
higher median CSF cell counts ( P = 0.04). Clinical parameters did not
differ between the subgroups with intrathecal GAD-ab synthesis and
without. Intrathecal GAD-ab synthesis did not seem to have an impact
for clinical outcome (Supplemental Table 2).
4. Discussion
Our analysis of SAINS-GAD + confirms previous findings in a large
multicentric setting and extends these by adding new aspects concerning
the current clinical management, the relevance of ab titers, and intra -
thecal GAD-ab synthesis.
4.1. Characteristics and management of patients with SAINS-GAD +

typical syndromes for suspected GAD-ab associated neurological

At first appearance, irrespective of GAD-ab levels, 45 out of 56 patients
(80%) presented with SAINS-GAD + . Transferred to our classification,
there were 45% of patients with E/LE, 9% with CAT, 16% with SPS, 11%
had an overlap [ 13 ]. The differences in syndrome distribution among
the described studies may possibly be attributed to an allocation bias, to
small sample sizes, or to the various test methods and criteria used.
In our cohort, 89% of the patients received immunotherapy, with
clinical improvement in 46%, but only 5% were free of any symptom at
last available follow-up. Preferences for individual immunotherapy
regimens varied among the clinical syndromes. Patients with E/LE were
predominantly treated with methylprednisolone pulses (80%), whereas
IVIG was used in a minority of these patients (8%). Conversely, IVIG was
frequently in the other SAINS-GAD + subgroups, mostly in patients with
SPS. These preferences are likely to reflect the existing literature refer -
ring to different ab-associated AINS rather than pathological consider -
ations [ 21 – 23 ]. In one of the rare randomized therapy studies in AINS,
the efficacy of IVIG was shown in a small cohort of GAD-ab associated
SPS patients [ 24 ]. This may be the reason for the frequent use of IVIG in
this particular SAINS-GAD + in our patients and in those of the Mayo
Clinic [ 20 ].
Immunotherapy response in our GAD-ab patients with CAT seemed
to be superior to that previously reported [ 25 ]. These differences
exemplarily reflect the multifaceted problems of retrospective studies
with uncontrolled treatment approaches, different outcome parameters
and variable follow-up periods. Given that SAINS-GAD + are chronic, the
positive immunotherapy responses could be attributed to the different
follow-up periods (3 – 153 months in our cohort vs. 37 – 124 months
previously [ 25 ]). In the Spanish study, several patients had overlap
syndrome, which sometimes appeared later in the course [ 25 ]. Thus, our
differentiation into the various syndromatic subgroups might be influ -
enced by the time of inclusion, and favorable immunotherapy response
might be to whether a “ pure ” AINS or an overlap is present.
4.2. Clinical relevance of high vs. low GAD-ab levels
Early studies reported serum GAD-ab levels of patients with pre -
sumed SAINS-GAD + to be 10-100fold higher than those of patients with
diabetes mellitus [ 1 ]. Nevertheless, high-GAD-ab patients with diabetes
mellitus without AINS and low-GAD-ab patients with AINS were re -
ported [ 3 , 26 , 27 ] questioning the validity of this approach. In
GENERATE, there are no inclusion prerequisites for GAD-ab levels.
Consecutively, a relevant proportion of SAINS-GAD + patients was
identified as low-GAD-ab. This was due to the typical clinical presen -
tation consistent with SAINS-GAD + and the absence of other etiologies
including other abs.
An ongoing shortcoming is the lack of definite and generally
accepted cut-off values for high- and low-GAD-ab levels for the different
laboratory test methods. The most widely accepted cut-off values in
clinical practice of GAD-abs were defined by Saiz [ 18 ]. The results of a
recent study investigating a total of 22 patients with positive serum
GAD-ab levels illustrate the existing problems in assessing the level of
GAD-ab. When applying a cut-off value for ELISA > 2000 U/mL, most
patients with GAD-ab levels above this threshold value had typical
SAINS-GAD + , whereas patients with lower GAD-ab levels had atypical
presentations. Nevertheless, 4/15 patients (27%) with typical SAINS-
GAD + had low GAD-ab levels (from 58 to 249 UI/mL), and one patient
with atypical presentation who had chronic inflammatory demyelin -
ating polyneuropathy had GAD-ab levels > 2000 U/mL. [ 28 ] To over -
come the existing shortcomings, Munoz-Lopetegi et al. sought to refine
the cut-off values and proposed levels > 10.000 U/mL in the serum by
ELISA for high-GAD-ab levels [ 13 ]. When applying these cut-off values,
94% of patients with high-GAD-ab levels had a SAINS-GAD + with
improvement under immunotherapy in 70% of cases. It is of particular
interest that there was still a proportion of 55% of patients below that
level presenting with SAINS-GAD + . Immunotherapy outcome of these
SAINS-GAD + patients was not reported [ 18 ]. Unfortunately, we could
not apply these proposed new cut-off values to our cohort because ab
levels were not titrated exactly to these heights in clinical standard tests
reflecting again difficulties in transferring results from scientific labo -
ratories into clinical practice. Other studies [ 15 , 20 ] used different cut-
off values or test units than those previously published and applied in
our study [ 14 , 25 ].
Of note, in 80% of SAINS-GAD + patients with low-GAD-ab were
found unmatched oligoclonal bands, thus presenting features of a
chronic inflammatory CNS syndrome by definition. One could argue that
the presence of unmatched oligoclonal bands may outweigh the low-

In sum, we assume that the current cut-off values for GAD-abs
determined by clinical tests may be less important for the distinction
whether GAD-abs are indicative for an autoimmune CNS disorder or not
in the context of SAINS-GAD + . It may also be conceivable that if in
doubt, a typical clinical presentation in the absence of evidence of other
etiologies overrules serology, given the methodological difficulties. Pa -
tients with suspected typical AINS should not be prematurely excluded
from further considerations only because of low-GAD-ab levels in clin -
ical routine tests. Possibly, the presence of unmatched oligoclonal bands
might compensate for a low-GAD-ab level. To avoid potentially harmful
over-treatment, it must be emphasized that we do not recommend
immunotherapy if there are low-GAD-abs without the presence of one of
the typical SAINS-GAD + .
4.3. Clinical relevance of intrathecal GAD-ab synthesis
Intrathecal GAD-ab synthesis was more frequent in SAINS-GAD +
with high-GAD-ab than with low-GAD-ab. Although it is intriguing to
assume that intrathecal GAD-ab synthesis could be an indicator for the
pathogenicity of GAD-abs in CNS diseases, data about this issue remain
scarce. The frequency of intrathecal GAD-ab synthesis in published
SAINS-GAD + patients varies. It was found in all patients with LE and
SPS [ 4 , 18 ], whereas it was infrequent in high-GAD-ab patients with E
[ 26 ]. Other studies failed to show correlations for CSF GAD-ab levels and
intrathecal GAD-ab synthesis with disease severity in SPS [ 16 ].
Recently, nineteen AINS patients with low-GAD-ab only in the CSF and
not in paired serum samples, equivalent with intrathecal GAD-ab syn -
thesis [ 27 ], were reported with improvement after immunotherapy in
57%, whereas none of the patients without immunotherapy did. In our
study, we found intrathecal GAD-ab synthesis in only 44%, and different
to the previous studies, most frequently in E/LE. The reasons for these
discrepancies are not apparent to us, a collection bias could be dis -
cussed. In sum, intrathecal GAD-ab synthesis may be a marker indicating
an autoimmune CNS disorder with GAD as a target antigen, but it did not
have prognostic value for clinical management in our cohort.
A recent review about GAD-abs in neurological syndromes war -
ranted that the presence of GAD-abs in patients with CNS disorders
cannot be taken synonymous with an ab-related autoimmune pathology
[ 19 ]. To avoid false positive judgements leading into overtherapy, the
authors proposed a therapeutic algorithm based on three parameters:
the serum ab levels, the type of AINS and the presence of intrathecal
GAD-ab synthesis. While we support this statement in principle, our data
did not show that these recommendations clearly resolve the existing
uncertainties concerning GAD-abs in AINS, but differing laboratory
methods and specifics of the cohorts studied need to be taken into
account.
4.4. Limitations
Our data are derived from a multicentric non-interventional registry
with all its inherent limitations. First, an allocation and reporting bias
has to be suspected. The lack of prerequisites for GAD-ab levels for
classification as SAINS-GAD + may represent a relevant weakness of the
data. Some patients might have been excluded on the basis of low GAD-
ab levels in some centers but not in others. On the other hand, our cohort
reflects the clinical reality in Germany. Despite low GAD-ab levels, pa -
tients were classified as immune-mediated and treated with immuno -
therapy in 94% of cases. In our opinion, the large number of cases of this
rare disease might outweigh the reporting bias to some extent. The
simultaneous occurrence of other abs is queried in GENERATE.
Although the presence of other abs in addition to GAD-abs was not
documented, we cannot fully exclude underreporting in this regard.
Second, due to the chronic course of SAINS-GAD + there was a high
heterogeneity in immunotherapy concerning substance preference and
sequence, dosage, duration, combination of therapies, and outcome
parameters, so that we are not able to reliably quantify the proportion of
the individual therapies. Third, a control group to assess immuno -
therapy benefit was lacking. Thus, we cannot exclude that improve -
ments may represent the natural disease course and the impact of
placebo effects. Fourth, outcome of SAINS-GAD + patients with seizures,
unlike other syndromes, can be influenced not only by immunotherapy
but the effect of antiseizure medication. Fifth, the outcome was assessed
using the mRS, a score originally designed for stroke patients. It does not
map all aspects equally well for all symptoms, e.g. seizures, but in the
absence of a more specific test, it is currently widely used as outcome
scale in AINS studies. Sixth, the inclusion of several serological test
methods from different laboratories poses inherent risks of data reli -
ability. We admit that these aspects reflect a relevant weakness in our
data and that the increasingly decentralised GAD-ab testing is worth
considering, but on the other hand, they also represent the current
clinical reality, as physicians in clinical practice make their therapeutic
decisions based on these test results. Data from recent studies indicate a
high interlaboratory and interprocedural reproducibility of ab test re -
sults in AINS [ 13 , 15 ]. Last, the data only allows the statement that in
patients with typical AINS, the GAD-ab level does not seem to have any
influence on the clinical picture, whereas in patients with a more un -
specific clinical picture, the significance of low GAD-ab remains unclear.
5. Conclusions
SAINS-GAD + comprised E/LE, CAT, SPS and an overlap. Immuno -
therapy was given with heterogeneous approaches and moderate effi -
cacy. The fact that a relevant number of patients with low-GAD-ab levels
were included highlights the difficulties in classifying laboratory results.
Patients suspected of SAINS-GAD + should not be excluded prematurely
from further management only because low-GAD-ab levels in clinical
routine tests. The presence of intrathecal GAD-ab synthesis in our cohort
did not affect clinical presentation or immunotherapy response, whereas
unmatched oligoclonal bands as a marker for a chronic inflammatory
CNS process might be relevant in patients with low-GAD-ab levels.
